title: War in Lebanon between Israel and Hezbollah, 2026

charter.in: The fighting in and over Lebanon between Israel and Hezbollah that began on 2 March 2026, after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran: Israeli air strikes, evacuation orders, demolitions and ground operations in Lebanon, Hezbollah fire into Israel, the Lebanese state's response, deaths and displacement in Lebanon, and talks or truces that cover the Lebanon front. Stories belong when Lebanon is their main subject, or (as optional) when a wider-war story gives the Lebanon front a major share.
out: The wider US/Israel-Iran war: strikes in Iran, Iranian missile fire on Israel and the Gulf states
Strait of Hormuz closure, shipping and Gulf energy
US-Iran talks, ceasefires and the June 2026 memorandum, except where they set terms for the Lebanon front
Gaza war and its October 2025 truce
Houthi attacks and the Yemen war
WHO emergency funding and World Health Assembly votes
charter.endEvent: A ceasefire on the Lebanon front that holds: Israeli strikes and ground operations in Lebanon and Hezbollah fire into Israel stop, with or without an Israeli withdrawal from the south. A truce or deal that our later stories show being broken by renewed strikes in Lebanon does not count.

figures.name: People killed in Lebanon
figures.definition: People killed in Lebanon since the fighting began on 2 March 2026, cumulative, as counted by Lebanese authorities (health ministry) or the UN. The counts do not separate civilians from fighters. Excludes deaths in Israel, Iran or elsewhere in the regional war, and tolls for a single day or strike.
variants: deaths in a single day or a single strike (e.g. 41 in 24 hours, 11 on Easter Sunday)
whole-war tolls across Iran, Lebanon and the Gulf (e.g. more than 7,000 dead)
subgroups such as children or medical workers killed

figures.name: People displaced in Lebanon
figures.definition: People forced from their homes inside Lebanon by the fighting since 2 March 2026, as counted by Lebanese authorities or the UN. A stock of displaced people, so it can fall as people return; our stories only ever report it rising or holding at about 1.2 million.
variants: residents covered by an evacuation order (e.g. roughly 400,000 in Beirut's southern suburbs)
people sheltering in collective sites only (e.g. over 130,000)
regional totals of refugees, internally displaced people and returnees (e.g. nearly 25 million)

notes: Start: our stories date the war from 2 March 2026 ('Since March 2'); the first story is 4 March. Not closed on 16 November 2026, and two events must not be read as the end. (1) The April truce: the 25 April story is the first to report it ('a fragile three‑week ceasefire', 'A temporary truce extended for three weeks'), without naming its parties; on 6 June the truces had 'cut major battles but not stopped strikes and deaths' and the Lebanon toll had risen from more than 2,400 to more than 3,500. (2) The 18 June US-Iran deal declared 'immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon', but the same day's UN story notes Israeli strikes on Beirut despite a ceasefire, Iran re-closed Hormuz on 22 June 'after Israeli attacks on Lebanon', strikes hit Nabatieh on 6 July, Israeli attacks 'continued in Gaza and Lebanon' on 4 October, the 2 November analysis describes 'Israel’s continued occupation and destruction of villages', and the 10 November story ('Trump says Iran fighting is over but keeps forces ready', not listed) names 'renewed conflict involving ... Israel in Lebanon'. After 25 April no story is mainly about Lebanon, so the later state comes only from optional entries and near misses. Counts: deaths are Lebanese health ministry or UN totals and do not separate civilians from fighters (6 June antifactor). Several stories restate a count loosely ('more than 1,000' after '1,029'; 'over one million' displaced after '1.2 million'); these are not falls. The 9 March 300,000 is given as displaced but the same story also says 'About 300,000 people were ordered to evacuate', so it may count only those under evacuation orders. The 7 March 400,000 is the population of the area under an evacuation order, not a displacement count. Near misses carry Lebanon numbers too (nearly 700,000 displaced on 10 March, 850 dead on 17 March, more than 900 dead and 800,000 displaced on 20 March, 1.2 million displaced on 6 June); a system that rightly leaves those stories out records none of them. Boundary rule used: optional when a wider-war story names Lebanon in its title or gives the Lebanon front a strand of its own with Lebanon-specific facts; near miss when Lebanon is a clause or one bullet in a list of fronts.
